issues.legal_issue: A successor in office of the public servant who promulgated an order is authorized to file the written complaint required to prosecute its disobedience.
material_facts: A proceeding concerning a land-possession dispute resulted in an order restraining one side from interfering with the other side’s possession.
The restrained persons allegedly disobeyed the order.
A successor magistrate filed a written complaint concerning the disobedience, and the High Court held that only the magistrate who had made the order could complain.
issues.conclusion: The successor in office falls within the meaning of the public servant concerned and may file the complaint; the High Court’s contrary ruling was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 195(1)(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires a written complaint by the public servant concerned, or by a public servant to whom that officer is administratively subordinate, before a court may take cognizance of the specified offences. The requirement is mandatory and protects against vexatious prosecutions; a written complaint is a prerequisite to proceedings for disobedience of a public order (Daulat Ram v. State of Punjab). Under Section 35(1) of the Code, a successor may exercise the powers and duties of the predecessor. Applying Ajaib Singh v. Joginder Singh, and consistent with the reasoning in P.D. Patel v. Emperor, Government Advocate, Bihar v. Kumar Singh, and Manik Lal Bhagat v. State, the Court held that the successor occupies the predecessor’s position for this purpose.

predicates.public_order_disobedience_case: The proceeding concerns an alleged disobedience of an order promulgated by a public servant.
predicates.written_complaint_filed_by_successor: A written complaint concerning the alleged disobedience was filed by the person who succeeded to the office of the public servant who promulgated the order.
predicates.successor_complaint_is_valid: A successor in office is authorized to file the required complaint concerning disobedience of the predecessor’s order.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns alleged disobedience of a public servant’s order and the successor in that office files a written complaint, the successor’s complaint is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A prolonged delay in proceedings may justify replacing an imprisonment sentence with an admonition.
material_facts: The respondents had been convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for disobeying a public order.
The proceedings began in 1968, and the High Court’s revision judgment was delivered in 1979 before the Supreme Court considered the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The respondents were admonished under Section 3 of the Probation of Offenders Act instead of being required to serve the imprisonment sentence.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 3 of the Probation of Offenders Act, the Court may admonish an offender instead of directing the offender to undergo imprisonment. In choosing that outcome, the Court relied on the substantial time that had elapsed during the proceedings.

predicates.criminal_appeal_after_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal concerning persons convicted of an offence and sentenced to imprisonment.
predicates.proceedings_substantially_delayed: A substantial period elapsed while the criminal proceedings were pending.
predicates.imprisonment_replaced_with_admonition: The offenders are admonished instead of being required to undergo the imprisonment sentence.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal after conviction, substantial delay in the proceedings may result in admonition replacing imprisonment.
